BRANCH PROTECTION DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your branch protection still match your own policy?

Someone disables a rule for one urgent hotfix — required reviews, admin enforcement, the force-push block — and nothing reminds anyone to turn it back on. It stays invisible until the rule is actually needed: a merge lands with no review, or a force push overwrites history nobody meant to lose. Paste your repo's actual settings and your declared policy below to find every rule that has quietly drifted weaker.

Nothing is uploaded. What you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — not even to read your branch protection settings for you.

1. Actual settings

Run gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection and paste the JSON output here.

2. Declared policy

JSON, or plain key: value lines — see the field list below the results.

Paste your actual settings and declared policy above, then click Check.

Findings

RuleStatusActualPolicy

Declared policy field reference

Every field is optional — a field you leave out is reported not policed, never assumed. Booleans: required_pull_request_reviews is entered as a plain required_approving_review_count number; the rest (require_code_owner_reviews, require_last_push_approval, enforce_admins, allow_force_pushes, allow_deletions, required_conversation_resolution, required_linear_history, required_signatures, strict_status_checks) are true/false. required_status_check_contexts is a comma-separated list (or a JSON array) of check names that must all be present — extra actual checks beyond the list are fine.

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection > actual.json
node cli.mjs --actual actual.json --policy policy.txt
node cli.mjs --actual actual.json --policy policy.txt --format json
node cli.mjs --actual actual.json --policy policy.txt --fail-on-drift   # exit 2 if anything drifted

Get cli.mjs — Node.js only, nothing to install, no network calls. Run it in CI right after a branch-protection or policy change to catch drift before it is needed.

Common questions

How does branch protection drift from what was intended?

Someone disables a rule for one urgent hotfix — turns off required reviews, or enables force pushes to fix a bad merge — and the settings page gives no reminder to turn it back on. Nothing breaks visibly until the next force push overwrites history, or the next merge lands with no review, on a rule everyone still believed was enforced.

Does this tool read my branch protection settings for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all. Fetch your own settings with gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection, paste the JSON in, write your declared policy in the second box, and the comparison happens entirely in this page.

What if my policy doesn't mention a rule?

It is reported as "not policed", never silently treated as a pass or a fail. A policy that only cares about force pushes says nothing about signed commits, and this tool will not invent an opinion your policy never stated.

What if the actual settings are stricter than the policy requires?

That is reported as "stronger than policy", not drift. Drift specifically means weaker than declared — more required reviewers than the policy demands, or an extra required status check, is never flagged as a problem.

Does a clean result mean my branch protection is fully correct?

No. It checks only the rules your own policy declares, against the specific fields GitHub's branch-protection API exposes. It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a review of whether the policy itself is any good.

More: why branch protection drifts silently, and how to stop finding out the hard way.

It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee about your repository's configuration, and it does not replace a qualified professional. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. What you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

A weakened branch-protection rule is one specific way a repository's own safeguards silently stop working. Required Checks Drift Check flags a required status check name nothing can ever satisfy again, and CODEOWNERS Shadow Check flags a review-requirement rule a later pattern silently overrides — two more slices of a setup that looks correct until you check.

vs-manually-checking-settings.html.text:
← Back to Branch Protection Drift Check

This checker vs. eyeballing Settings → Branches

The ordinary way anyone checks branch protection is opening a repository's Settings → Branches page and reading the toggles, or running gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection and skimming the JSON. That confirms a rule is present -- required reviews are on, force pushes are off.

It does not confirm a rule still says what your team agreed it should say. A required review count quietly dropped from 2 to 1 during an incident still reads as "required reviews: on". A required status check left over from a CI job that was renamed six months ago still reads as "status checks: required" -- it just can never be satisfied again, because nothing produces a check with that exact name anymore. Both look identical to a glance and identical in the raw JSON unless you compare every field against a separate, written record of what it should be.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Confirm a rule exists at all right now -- is anything protecting this branch. Settings → Branches, or gh api ... /protection -- this checker does not replace looking at your own settings; it needs you to fetch them first.
Change a setting. Settings → Branches, or the GitHub API -- this checker only compares, it never writes anything back to GitHub.
Notice a required review count silently dropped from 2 to 1, or admin enforcement quietly turned off. This checker -- both still read as "on" at a glance; only a field-by-field diff against a written policy catches the drop.
Catch a required status check name left over from a renamed or deleted CI job. This checker -- the settings page shows the string is required, not whether any job still produces a check with that exact name.
Get a written record of what the policy should be, not just what it currently is. This checker -- typing a policy once (see the field reference on the tool itself) gives you something durable to diff against next time, instead of relying on memory of the last time someone looked.
Run the same comparison automatically after every branch-protection or policy change. This checker's CLI (cli.mjs --fail-on-drift) -- reading the settings page by eye does not scale to "every change, automatically".

These are not competitors. You still fetch the actual settings from GitHub yourself -- this tool makes no network calls of its own and never reads your branch protection for you. What it replaces is the part eyeballing the settings page cannot do at all: comparing every field against a separate written policy and naming, specifically, which ones no longer match.

Common questions

Isn't it faster to just look at Settings → Branches myself?

For confirming a rule exists at all, yes — open the page, see the toggle, done. This tool answers a different question: does every field still match what your team actually agreed the policy should be? A required review count that was quietly dropped from 2 to 1, or a required status check name left over from a renamed CI job, still shows as "on" in the UI. Reading the page confirms the rule is present; it does not confirm the rule still says what you think it says.

What does eyeballing the settings page actually miss?

Anything where the field is set but wrong rather than unset. The count under required approving reviews, whether Require approval of the most recent push is on, which named status checks are required (a renamed or deleted CI job leaves a required check nothing can ever satisfy, invisible unless you compare the exact string), and whether admin enforcement is on all look identical to a glance — a settings screen shows their current value, not whether that value still matches a decision your team wrote down somewhere else.

Do I need to write down a policy before I can use this?

Only informally — a few key: value lines are enough (see the field reference on the tool itself), and you can paste the actual settings first and treat that as your policy draft going forward. The comparison is only as useful as the policy is accurate, the same way reading the settings page is only as useful as your memory of what they should say.

Is this a replacement for reading the branch protection settings?

No — you still fetch the actual settings yourself, with gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection or the Settings → Branches page, and this tool never reads them for you. It replaces the field-by-field comparison against a written policy, not the act of looking at your repository's settings.

why-branch-protection-drifts.html.text:
← Back to Branch Protection Drift Check

Why branch protection drifts silently

Most configuration in a software project lives in a file: a linter's rule set, a CI workflow, an environment's variable list. All of it goes through version control, so a change to it is a diff someone reviews before it takes effect, and a change nobody meant to make is visible in git blame forever.

GitHub branch protection is not that. It lives in repository settings — a live control panel a maintainer edits directly, with no commit, no pull request, and no reviewer. The audit log records that a setting changed and who changed it, but nothing compares the new state to what the team actually agreed the policy should be. There is no diff to notice, because there was never a file to diff.

The ordinary way it happens

It is rarely a decision to weaken security. It is an incident: production is down, the fix is ready, and required reviews or a status check are standing between the fix and the deploy. Someone with admin access turns the rule off, ships the fix, and means to turn it back on once things calm down. The incident ends; the follow-up task to re-enable the rule does not get the same urgency the incident itself had, and it quietly falls off the list.

Months later, a different change — one that genuinely needed review — merges without it, because the rule that would have required a review has been off the whole time. Nobody decided that outcome. Nobody would have agreed to it if asked directly. It happened because the gap between the setting changing and the setting mattering can be arbitrarily long, and nothing in GitHub's own UI narrows that gap by reminding anyone what is currently off.

Why "read the settings page" doesn't fix it

The settings page shows the current state accurately. What it cannot show is whether the current state matches what your team decided the policy should be, because GitHub has no concept of your declared policy — only of whatever the toggles currently say. Reading the page tells you the branch is unprotected in some way; it does not tell you that unprotected way is a deviation from anything, unless you already remember, precisely, what every toggle used to be.

That is the gap a declared policy closes: write down, once, what every rule is supposed to be — required reviewer count, admin enforcement, force-push and deletion rules, required status checks — and compare the live settings against that written statement whenever you have reason to check, rather than against memory.

What to actually do about it

  1. Write the policy down once, in whatever form your team will actually maintain — a paragraph in a wiki, a YAML file in the repo, or just the plain-text field list this tool accepts.
  2. After any incident that involved touching branch protection, check the live settings against that policy as part of the incident's own follow-up — not as a separate task that competes for priority once the pressure is off.
  3. Run the comparison periodically regardless — in CI on a schedule, or by hand before a compliance review — because an incident is not the only way a setting can be that no diff would ever have surfaced.

Compare your own repository's actual settings against a declared policy →
